one_line: A five-stage workflow for building a site with Claude Design: write a design.md brand file first, build a design system from it, wireframe, produce the full design, then hand off to Claude Code with a Supabase backend.
summary: The host walks through a process for using Claude Design (Anthropic's design tool, launched as a research preview with Opus 4.7) to build a multi-page project-management site. The core claim is that a design.md brand file written before any Claude Design prompting keeps output on-brand and avoids the generic styling that models fall back to when they build a design system unaided. A planning skill run in Claude Code interviews the user, writes design.md, and validates it, and the host suggests previewing the file in a visualizer so that design iterations do not burn Claude Design tokens. The design system is then created from the file, followed by wireframes with several variants per screen and comment-based batched edits, and then the full visual design built on the chosen wireframe. Handoff to Claude Code goes through the Claude Design MCP, which works in both directions. A deep review of design.md against the built code caught responsiveness problems that were then fixed. The app's persistence is added with Supabase, using its agent skills and its MCP server rather than the CLI. The video is a practitioner tutorial with concrete steps, but it gives few measurements, and it closes with a plug for the host's paid community, where the skill is distributed.

key_ideas.idea: Write a design.md brand file before prompting Claude Design. Without it, a generated design system falls back to the generic colors and styles the Opus models default to, so the site looks like other AI-built sites.
key_ideas.detail: The host frames design.md as a Google-originated format that the coding agent reads before writing anything. Its main benefits are control and consistency across pages, since every page derives from one file.

key_ideas.idea: A planning skill run in Claude Code produces design.md. It interviews the user about visual identity, writes the file, validates it against Google's format with scripts, and carries anti-slop reference patterns.
key_ideas.detail: The host ran the skill through a slash command with a broad app description. Colors can be supplied or chosen by the model. Coolors is used to build and export a palette as code text that is pasted into the file.

key_ideas.idea: Preview design.md in a visualizer before using Claude Design. Each design.md revision made after seeing output in Claude Design costs tokens.
key_ideas.detail: The host uses designmd.space to see how colors and elements interact. Reference brands from getdesign.md can serve as a starting point instead of an original file.

key_ideas.idea: Wireframe before the full design. Claude Design is slow to generate, so a wrong structure is expensive to fix after the full build.
key_ideas.detail: Wireframes are built on the design system with a screen count. Multiple variants per screen are generated and compared. Comments on individual elements carry exact element context, and the host advises batching them so they are resolved in one pass.

key_ideas.idea: Full-design output needs manual fixes. Button colors are often wrong, and the output is sparse, so textures and elements have to be requested.
key_ideas.detail: Small deletions can be applied directly on the canvas, which avoids a prompt and its token cost. A final polish prompt adds subtle refinements. Animations are requested separately with an instruction to keep them subtle.

key_ideas.idea: The Claude Design to Claude Code handoff goes through the Claude Design MCP and works in both directions. The agent reads metadata, then the file list, then the design system, then each element, before building.
key_ideas.detail: The host reports that a deep review comparing design.md with the built code found responsiveness problems (mobile and tablet), which the host attributes to Claude Design output being tuned to one screen size.

key_ideas.idea: Persistence needs a real backend. The host uses Supabase, installed as an agent skill bundle with a general skill and a best-practices skill that triggers on optimize-performance requests. The schema was pre-made and placed in the project root so the agent would not design it.
key_ideas.detail: The skill is only instructions and cannot change a remote project, so the agent needs a connection. The host chose the Supabase MCP over the CLI because it avoids handling login keys. Authentication happens in the browser. The agent then ran tests against the database requests and locked down data that users should not reach.

techniques.name: design.md-first planning skill
techniques.how: In Claude Code, invoke the planning skill's slash command with a broad description of the app. Answer its questions about visual identity and palette (a palette can be exported from Coolors as code text and pasted in). Let it write design.md and run its validation scripts. Keep anti-slop references loaded. The skill was installed by pasting the GitHub link into Claude Code and asking it to set the skill up in the project's .claude folder. The video does not name the skill.
techniques.when: Before any Claude Design work on a new brand or product, to prevent generic model-default styling and to keep multi-page output consistent.

techniques.name: Preview design.md outside the token-metered tool
techniques.how: Load design.md into a visualizer (the host names designmd.space) and check palette roles and element styling. Revise the file there, and only then generate in Claude Design.
techniques.when: When iterating on a brand is expensive in Claude Design's 5-hour token budget.

techniques.name: Design system from design.md
techniques.how: In Claude Design, create a new design system and upload design.md as an asset. Claude Design generates the system from the file through a to-do list.
techniques.when: After design.md is locked, before wireframes or any screens.

techniques.name: Wireframe, then batched comments
techniques.how: Select the design system, choose the wireframe option, and prompt with the screen count. Generate multiple variants per screen, then add comments by selecting the comment tool and clicking the exact element. Group the comments and send them together.
techniques.when: To settle layout and structure before paying for full visual generation.

techniques.name: Full design from a chosen wireframe
techniques.how: Pick the variant by its code number. Prompt for full-detail screens that keep the wireframe layout and spacing. Fix buttons and accents with comments, use on-canvas edits for small removals, then run a polish prompt. Ask for textures or elements if the result is sparse.
techniques.when: After the wireframe structure is approved.

techniques.name: Claude Design to Claude Code handoff
techniques.how: Use the Claude Design MCP export and paste the generated handoff prompt into Claude Code. The agent reads metadata, lists project files, reads the design system first, then reads each element and builds the app. Round trips work in the reverse direction as well.
techniques.when: When the design is final and needs to become a real app.

techniques.name: Post-build design.md conformance review
techniques.how: Ask Claude Code for a deep review that checks design.md against the built code, paying attention to responsiveness at mobile and tablet sizes. Apply the fixes it reports.
techniques.when: Right after handoff, before adding backend functionality.

techniques.name: Supabase skill install and MCP connection
techniques.how: Copy the Supabase install command for your agent and run it in the project terminal. This installs two skills: a general Supabase skill (triggered by database or login tasks) and a best-practices skill (triggered by optimize-performance in a prompt). Connect the MCP with the MCP slash command in Claude Code, select authenticate, and log in in the browser. Prefer the MCP over the CLI to avoid storing login keys. Put a pre-made schema in the project root before prompting the agent to connect the UI to the backend.
techniques.when: When an app built from a design needs persistent data and user access control.

numbers.claim: Claude Design usage is capped by a 5-hour window shared with all other Claude usage, with a token cap inside the window. Once the cap is hit, the user waits for the window to reset.
The host's team runs Opus 5 at medium effort for design work to limit token burn. Opus is described as the best for design but token-heavy, and Haiku uses fewer tokens but may need more refinement.
The five-stage process covers design.md, design system, wireframes, full design, and handoff/backend. The Supabase bundle contains two skills.
Claude Design launched as a research preview alongside Opus 4.7 and is available on all paid plans. Its scope covers websites, slides, documents, and animations.

hot_takes: Design systems generated without a design.md drift to the same generic AI styles. The speaker's claim, not measured.
Iterating inside Claude Design is token-expensive, so previewing design.md in a separate visualizer is the cheaper loop.
Claude Design output is tuned to one screen size, so responsive fixes are needed after handoff. The host says this is because the tool is early.
The video promotes the host's paid community (AI LABS Pro) as the distribution point for the design skill. It is not a sponsored segment, and the substance is concrete enough to keep quality at 3.

relevance.why: AgentOS has no stated web UI. The design.md-first pattern is only relevant if a dashboard or docs site gets built.
relevance.action: If AgentOS needs a web dashboard, generate its style from a validated spec file written first, not from a generator's defaults.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI. The interview-then-write-validated-spec planning skill and the MCP connection pattern are relevant to its plan step, but design is not.
relevance.action: Compare the design.md planning skill (interview, write spec, validate with scripts, load anti-pattern references) with ProsHarness's plan step to see if its plan artifact should be validated the same way.
